justification_text:
My point estimates reflected a modestly bullish near-term outlook anchored around the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, with very little drift built in over the short horizon. For the one-day estimate, I essentially assumed mean-reversion tendencies and low overnight volatility would keep the price close to the last observed level, with only a marginal upward drift reflecting the slight positive bias historically observed in equity markets on a daily basis. The one-week estimate incorporated a similarly small positive drift, while the one-month estimate nudged slightly higher to account for the long-run equity risk premium compounding over a longer window. None of these horizons assumed any specific catalysts; rather, they reflected a baseline expectation of continuity in the prevailing trend.

The confidence interval widths were primarily driven by realized and implied volatility assumptions appropriate to each time horizon. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because daily price moves in a large-cap stock or index-tracking instrument tend to be constrained barring major surprises. At one week, the interval widens to capture the accumulation of daily uncertainties, scheduled macroeconomic releases, and potential earnings or policy announcements. At one month, the interval becomes substantially wider because a full month introduces the possibility of regime shifts, Federal Reserve communications, earnings seasons, and geopolitical developments that are difficult to anticipate. The interval widths essentially scaled with the square root of time, a standard approach rooted in the random-walk properties of financial prices.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharply weaker jobs report, an unexpected credit event, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions — could produce a swift sell-off that breaches the lower bound even at the one-week horizon. A sudden shift in Federal Reserve rhetoric toward more aggressive tightening could similarly compress valuations quickly. On the upside, a strong earnings surprise, a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical conflict, or a dovish pivot in central bank communication could push prices well above the upper bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon where the range is already wider but still cannot fully capture tail scenarios driven by unexpected positive news flow.

It is also worth noting that liquidity conditions and market microstructure can occasionally amplify moves beyond what volatility models predict. During periods of low liquidity — such as around major holidays or in the immediate aftermath of a shock — bid-ask spreads widen and price discovery becomes noisier, which can temporarily push prices outside statistically derived intervals before they revert. My stated intervals should therefore be interpreted as capturing the central 90% of plausible outcomes under relatively normal market functioning, not as hard boundaries under all conceivable conditions.
